01 · Research

Selected research.

Two questions drive me: can image-derived features become interpretable phenotypes that link genetic variation to changes in tissue, and which cell–cell interactions drive disease states rather than merely accompany them? Each project below brought me to the same boundary: results that are suggestive but not yet tested.

01 / 04Simulated truth

Know the answer, then test.

Real single-cell data has no answer key, so we made one. Using Splatter, with parameters estimated from real 10x samples, we simulated datasets of 10k to 1M cells across 12 known populations. Then we ran 170 end-to-end workflows across Seurat, SingleCellExperiment and Scanpy, covering normalization, feature selection, dimensionality reduction and clustering. We then validated the selected workflows on a real lung tumour/normal dataset, where no ground-truth labels exist.

The main lesson: good clustering scores do not guarantee that the true cell populations are recovered.

Robustness Benchmarking of scRNA-seq Pipelines for Tumor Microenvironment Profiling

02 / 04Real tumours

When the labels run out.

We profiled 17 neuroblastoma samples, resolving 16 clusters across nine cell types, including six distinct tumour subpopulations and a rare plasma cell population.

Without ground truth, independent lines of evidence have to agree. We used ligand–receptor modelling (13 core pathways) to map tumour–immune crosstalk, and inferCNV to tie transcriptional states to chromosomal changes such as MYCN-associated 2p gains. Trajectory analysis pointed to convergent developmental programs rather than a single lineage.

Linking predicted ligand–receptor interactions to tumour signalling pathways left me with the question I want to answer next: which of these interactions are functionally important?

Under review · Scientific Reports · second author
Integrated Single-Cell Profiling Highlights Developmental Origins, Intercellular Signaling, and Genomic Programs in Neuroblastoma

Tumour subpopulations, cell–cell signalling and copy-number programs in neuroblastoma.

03 / 04Interpretability

94% accurate, until you split by patient.

For our undergraduate thesis we designed a dual-branch 2D CNN, with small- and large-kernel stacks, to classify Alzheimer's disease, MCI and healthy controls from T1-weighted MRI (ADNI, 505 subjects, 1:23.7 class imbalance). It reached 94% accuracy on MRI slices. In my postgraduate work, I re-evaluated it with a participant-level split, so that slices from the same person could no longer appear in both training and test sets, and balanced accuracy fell to 60–75%. That taught me how easily performance can mislead without careful validation.

It also made me ask whether explanations highlight meaningful anatomy. Standard tools didn't work with the dual-branch architecture, so we built EfficientMCIAnalyzer, which generates LIME heatmaps and splits predictions into four misclassification sub-classes to check whether the model relies on clinically relevant regions or on imaging artifacts.

Undergraduate thesis · ITIDA-funded
An Interpretable 2D Dual-CNN Framework for Alzheimer's Disease Detection from Structural MRI Slices

Supervised by Dr. Eman Badr. One of 189 projects funded nationwide by the ITAC program.

04 / 04Causal inference

From association to cause.

Before an imaging phenotype can be tested against genetic variation, it has to be defined. In DiagNexus, we benchmarked the model against VGG-16 transfer learning and used LIME and SHAP to localise discriminative regions. We then linked those regional volumes to ADNI genetic variants with LASSO regression and two-stage least-squares Mendelian randomization.

Manuscript in preparation · co-first author
DiagNexus: An Interpretable CNN-Based CAD System for Early Alzheimer's Diagnosis and Genetic Risk Analysis

Extends the thesis model from prediction towards genetic risk.
